<reason>Both sides built genuinely strong, well-structured cases, and CON's core strategic move — detaching "meaningful review" (reasons, data correction, power to reverse) from the requirement that the decider be human — was a smart and original reframe that scored real points on backlog and rubber-stamp risks. But PRO correctly pressed that CON's own standard collapses back into requiring a human the moment the dispute is a genuine judgment call (credibility, discretion, context) rather than a factual data mismatch. CON's rebuttals repeatedly worked for the "wrong wage file" case but never squarely explained who or what performs "engagement with evidence" and "power to reverse" in a contested credibility or discretion case. PRO's closing (A5) sharpened exactly this gap, and CON's closing (B5) responded mainly by reasserting the backlog/scarcity narrative and even conceded ground by saying attention should be "reserved" and "targeted" for complex cases — which is functionally PRO's own narrowed formulation of the right. PRO also answered the backlog objection with a concrete due-process mechanism (continued benefits pending review, statutory clock, state bears delay cost) and the public defender analogy, which CON's response weakened but did not fully neutralize. PRO's opening was clipped for length, a real execution cost, but the substantive content survived intact. On balance PRO ends the debate with the cleaner, more resolved path to victory.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A4.3–A4.5 and A5.1–A5.4: PRO's argument that CON's own "reasons + power to reverse" standard, when applied to genuinely contested judgment calls, functionally requires a human decider — a point CON's closing (B5) never directly rebutted, instead pivoting back to the backlog/scarcity framing and quietly conceding that attention should be "reserved" for complex cases.</best_rebuttal>
